column1: A day on Venus is longer than its year
column2: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only about 225 to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.
column3: Our idea of a day is only local.

column1: There are more stars than grains of sand on Earth's beaches
column2: Astronomers estimate around 10^22 to 10^24 stars in the observable universe. That likely outnumbers all the sand grains on Earth's beaches.
column3: Scale in space defeats intuition.

column1: Footprints on the Moon could last millions of years
column2: The Moon has no wind or rain to erase them. Unless a meteorite hits, the Apollo astronauts' bootprints will stay for a very long time.
column3: Without weather, history stays put.

column1: Space is not completely silent to instruments
column2: Sound cannot travel through the near-vacuum of space. But spacecraft record radio waves and plasma vibrations that scientists convert into sound.
column3: Translation reveals hidden signals.

column1: Saturn would float in a big enough bath
column2: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. In a hypothetical ocean large enough, it would float.
column3: Giant does not always mean heavy for its size.

column1: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us
column2: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second. From the Sun to Earth, that takes around 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
column3: When you look at the sky, you see the past.

column1: The International Space Station orbits every 90 minutes
column2: The ISS travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. Astronauts on board see around 16 sunrises and sunsets a day.
column3: Speed changes even the rhythm of a day.

column1: Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system
column2: Olympus Mons is about 22 kilometres high, more than twice the height of Everest above sea level. Its base is roughly the size of Poland.
column3: Low gravity lets mountains grow huge.

column1: Astronauts grow taller in space
column2: Without gravity compressing the spine, astronauts can gain up to about 3 percent in height. They shrink back after returning to Earth.
column3: Gravity shapes our bodies every day.

column1: A year on Neptune lasts 165 Earth years
column2: Neptune is so far from the Sun that it takes about 165 years to complete one orbit. It completed its first orbit since discovery in 2011.
column3: Distance stretches time.

column1: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm
column2: The storm is wider than Earth and has been observed for at least 150 years. It has been shrinking in recent decades.
column3: Some storms outlast centuries.

column1: The Moon is slowly drifting away
column2: Laser measurements show the Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further from Earth each year. That is about as fast as fingernails grow.
column3: Tiny changes add up over billions of years.

column1: You could fit all the planets between Earth and the Moon
column2: The average Earth–Moon distance is about 384,400 kilometres. The diameters of all the other planets add up to slightly less than that.
column3: Space between things is vast.

column1: Pluto is smaller than the Moon
column2: Pluto's diameter is about 2,377 kilometres, while the Moon's is about 3,475. It was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
column3: Categories change as we learn more.

column1: Mercury is not the hottest planet
column2: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury is beaten by Venus. Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping it above 460°C.
column3: Insulation matters more than distance.

column1: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old
column2: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background put the age of the universe at roughly 13.8 billion years. Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
column3: We are newcomers in a very old story.

column1: Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object
column2: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. It carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.
column3: A message in a bottle, sent across the stars.

column1: Some planets orbit two suns
column2: Astronomers have found planets orbiting pairs of stars. Kepler-16b, found in 2011, was the first clear example.
column3: Science fiction keeps turning into science.

column1: Neutron stars can spin hundreds of times a second
column2: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radiation across space. The fastest known spin over 700 times a second.
column3: Collapse can create extreme spin.

column1: There is a giant cloud of alcohol in space
column2: Sagittarius B2, a gas cloud near the centre of our galaxy, contains large amounts of ethyl alcohol. It is spread too thin to be drinkable.
column3: Chemistry happens everywhere.

column1: The Sun makes up 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass
column2: All the planets, moons and asteroids together are a tiny fraction. Jupiter holds most of what is left.
column3: One giant dominates the family.

column1: Black holes do not suck everything in
column2: From a distance, a black hole's gravity behaves like any object of the same mass. Only very close in, past the event horizon, is escape impossible.
column3: Myths exaggerate the danger.

column1: Mars has blue sunsets
column2: Fine dust in the Martian atmosphere scatters blue light forward around the Sun. Rovers have photographed bluish sunsets.
column3: Different air paints a different sky.

column1: A spoonful of the Sun's core would be scorching
column2: The Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius. Nuclear fusion there turns hydrogen into helium.
column3: Stars are nuclear furnaces.

column1: Earth is closest to the Sun in January
column2: Earth's orbit is slightly oval. It reaches its closest point, perihelion, in early January, during northern winter.
column3: Seasons come from tilt, not distance.

column1: The Moon has moonquakes
column2: Seismometers left by Apollo astronauts recorded quakes on the Moon. Some shallow ones lasted for minutes.
column3: Even quiet worlds can shake.

column1: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way
column2: Estimates put Earth's trees at around 3 trillion. The Milky Way holds roughly 100 to 400 billion stars.
column3: Our planet holds its own vast numbers.

column1: Uranus spins on its side
column2: Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so it rolls around the Sun. Each pole gets around 42 years of continuous sunlight.
column3: A single collision can change a planet forever.

column1: The Sun is a middle-aged star
column2: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old. It is expected to shine for roughly another 5 billion years.
column3: Our star is only halfway through its story.

column1: Comets have two tails
column2: A comet often has a curved dust tail and a straight ion tail. The ion tail always points away from the Sun.
column3: Solar wind shapes what we see.

column1: The Moon always shows the same face
column2: The Moon spins once for every orbit of Earth, so the same side always faces us. This is called tidal locking.
column3: Gravity can sync rhythms.

column1: The far side of the Moon is not dark
column2: It gets as much sunlight as the near side. It was simply unseen until a Soviet probe photographed it in 1959.
column3: Hidden is not the same as dark.

column1: Space smells, according to astronauts
column2: Astronauts have described a smell like seared steak or hot metal on their suits after spacewalks.
column3: Space has a scent, even without air.

column1: Mars has two small moons
column2: Phobos and Deimos are small and irregular. Phobos is slowly spiralling inwards and may break apart in tens of millions of years.
column3: Even moons have lifespans.

column1: The Milky Way will merge with Andromeda
column2: In about 4 to 5 billion years, our galaxy and Andromeda are expected to collide and merge. Stars are so far apart they rarely hit each other.
column3: Even collisions can be peaceful at scale.

column1: Jupiter has the most massive moon system
column2: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury.
column3: Some moons outsize planets.

column1: Saturn's rings are mostly ice
column2: The rings are made largely of water ice chunks, from tiny grains to boulders. They are very wide but often only tens of metres thick.
column3: Huge structures can be incredibly thin.

column1: A light year measures distance, not time
column2: It is the distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.
column3: Some words trick us with their names.

column1: The first animal in orbit was a dog
column2: Laika orbited Earth aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957. She did not survive the mission.
column3: Progress has had real costs.

column1: Astronauts lose bone mass in space
column2: Without gravity, bones lose density. Astronauts exercise for about two hours a day to limit the loss.
column3: Gravity keeps us strong.

column1: Venus is the hottest planet
column2: Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping surface temperatures around 465°C.
column3: Atmosphere can matter more than distance.

column1: Mercury has ice
column2: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury may have water ice in shadowed craters at its poles.
column3: Extremes can sit side by side.

column1: The Sun is mostly hydrogen
column2: By mass, the Sun is about 73 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium, with traces of other elements.
column3: Stars are built from the simplest stuff.

column1: There may be a planet with diamond rain
column2: Scientists think the extreme pressures inside Neptune and Uranus may turn carbon into diamonds that sink like rain.
column3: Weather can be stranger than fiction.

column1: Shooting stars are tiny
column2: Most meteors are grains of dust or sand that burn up in the atmosphere. They glow because they hit the air at huge speed.
column3: Small things can make big displays.

column1: Earth gets heavier from space dust
column2: Tens of thousands of tonnes of cosmic dust fall on Earth every year.
column3: The sky is always falling, slowly.

column1: Pluto has a heart
column2: NASA's New Horizons spacecraft found a huge heart-shaped region of nitrogen ice on Pluto in 2015.
column3: Distant worlds can surprise us.

column1: Olympus Mons would be hard to see from its base
column2: It is so broad that its slopes curve away over the horizon. From the base you could not see the summit.
column3: Scale can make giants invisible.

column1: The ISS is visible from the ground
column2: The International Space Station often looks like a bright, steady star moving across the sky.
column3: You can watch people living in space.

column1: There is no up or down in space
column2: In orbit, astronauts float freely and arrange equipment on every surface.
column3: Orientation is just a convention.

column1: The Sun's light is white
column2: The Sun gives off all colours of visible light, which combine to white. It looks yellow because of our atmosphere.
column3: The sky changes how we see.

column1: Mars has seasons
column2: Mars is tilted like Earth, so it has seasons. They last about twice as long because its year is longer.
column3: Familiar patterns appear on other worlds.

column1: Europa may have an ocean
column2: Jupiter's moon Europa is thought to have a salty ocean beneath its icy crust. It is a target in the search for life.
column3: Life may hide under ice.

column1: The asteroid belt is mostly empty
column2: Asteroids are far apart, often hundreds of thousands of kilometres. Spacecraft fly through without trouble.
column3: Sci-fi crowds space too much.

column1: A spacesuit is like a personal spacecraft
column2: It provides oxygen, pressure, temperature control and protection from radiation and dust.
column3: Survival needs a lot of kit.

column1: We have only seen one side of the Milky Way
column2: Because we are inside it, we cannot photograph the whole galaxy. Pictures of it are illustrations or other galaxies.
column3: Some views are impossible from inside.

column1: Solar eclipses happen by coincidence
column2: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times further away. So they look the same size.
column3: A cosmic coincidence gives us eclipses.

column1: Saturn's moon Titan has lakes
column2: Titan has lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane. It also has rain and a thick atmosphere.
column3: Familiar landscapes can form from alien stuff.

column1: The first person in space was Yuri Gagarin
column2: On 12 April 1961, Gagarin orbited Earth once in Vostok 1. The flight lasted about 108 minutes.
column3: One orbit changed the world.

column1: Twelve people have walked on the Moon
column2: Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo missions.
column3: A small club with a giant achievement.

column1: Space is cold, but not everywhere
column2: In shadow, objects can get extremely cold. In direct sunlight they can get very hot, so spacecraft need thermal control.
column3: Extremes depend on where you stand.

column1: The Andromeda galaxy is visible without a telescope
column2: On a dark night it looks like a faint smudge. It is about 2.5 million light years away.
column3: You can see another galaxy with your own eyes.

column1: The Moon makes Earth's tides
column2: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, creating bulges. The Sun contributes too, making spring and neap tides.
column3: Distant objects shape our daily lives.

column1: Earth's magnetic field protects us
column2: It deflects much of the solar wind. Without it, our atmosphere could slowly be stripped away.
column3: Invisible shields matter.

column1: Auroras are caused by the solar wind
column2: Charged particles from the Sun collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, making the sky glow.
column3: Space weather paints the sky.

column1: Black holes can spin
column2: Many black holes rotate, some at close to the maximum possible speed. Spin affects how matter falls in.
column3: Even the darkest objects move.

column1: The Kármán line marks where space begins
column2: It is commonly set at 100 kilometres above sea level. Some organisations use 80 kilometres instead.
column3: Boundaries are often agreed, not natural.

column1: Space junk is a growing problem
column2: Thousands of defunct satellites and fragments orbit Earth. Collisions can create more debris.
column3: Every launch leaves a trace.

column1: The first image of a black hole came in 2019
column2: The Event Horizon Telescope linked telescopes worldwide to image the black hole in galaxy M87.
column3: Teamwork can see the invisible.

column1: Hubble has been in orbit since 1990
column2: The Hubble Space Telescope has made over a million observations. It was repaired by astronauts several times.
column3: Maintenance can extend a mission for decades.

column1: Light from the Moon is reflected sunlight
column2: The Moon makes no light of its own. It reflects only around 12 percent of the sunlight that hits it.
column3: Even brightness can be borrowed.

column1: A day on Mars is about 24 hours 40 minutes
column2: A Martian day is called a sol. Rover teams on Earth have worked on Mars time.
column3: Some alien rhythms feel familiar.

column1: Stars come in many colours
column2: Hotter stars look blue-white, cooler ones look red. The Sun is a medium-temperature yellow-white star.
column3: Colour reveals temperature.

column1: Jupiter protects Earth, partly
column2: Its gravity can deflect some comets and asteroids, though it can also send others towards the inner solar system.
column3: Big neighbours have mixed effects.

column1: Most of the universe is invisible
column2: Ordinary matter makes up only about 5 percent of the universe. The rest is dark matter and dark energy.
column3: We understand only a small slice.

column1: Space has a speed record holder
column2: NASA's Parker Solar Probe became the fastest human-made object, travelling hundreds of thousands of kilometres per hour near the Sun.
column3: Gravity can be a slingshot.

column1: The Moon formed from a collision, most likely
column2: The leading theory says a Mars-sized body hit early Earth, and debris formed the Moon.
column3: Violent beginnings can create beauty.

column1: Spacecraft use gravity assists
column2: Probes swing past planets to gain speed and change direction without extra fuel.
column3: Clever paths save energy.

column1: Galaxies come in shapes
column2: Astronomers classify galaxies as spiral, elliptical or irregular. The Milky Way is a barred spiral.
column3: Patterns help us understand the vast.

column1: The Sun loses mass every second
column2: Through fusion and solar wind, the Sun loses millions of tonnes of mass each second. It has plenty to spare.
column3: Even giants spend.

column1: Astronauts' voices sound normal inside the station
column2: The ISS is filled with air, so sound travels as normal. Only in the vacuum outside is there silence.
column3: Silence needs a vacuum.

column1: Exoplanets number in the thousands
column2: Over 5,000 planets outside our solar system have been confirmed. Many more are likely.
column3: Planets are common.

column1: Venus has no moons
column2: Venus and Mercury are the only planets in our solar system without moons.
column3: Not every planet has company.

column1: The Great Bear is not a constellation's full story
column2: The Plough, or Big Dipper, is part of the larger constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear.
column3: Familiar shapes can be pieces of bigger pictures.
